questions.title: The bottleneck moves after adoption
questions.stem: An assistant halves order-entry time, but adoption is 30%. The warehouse is at capacity and shipment time is unchanged. Leadership wants broader category coverage to speed shipments. What should discovery test FIRST?

options.text: Improve substitution explanations and use increased adoption to predict shorter shipment times.
options.why: The warehouse bottleneck invalidates the assumed proportional gain.

options.text: Measure stage times, adoption and warehouse queues to test whether expansion can speed shipments.
options.why: This tests the business bottleneck before expanding capability.

options.text: Expand categories in one branch and use adoption as the main evidence of shipment improvement.
options.why: Adoption alone cannot establish shipment-time improvement.

options.text: Compare larger-model entry accuracy to identify which product categories should receive expansion.
options.why: Accuracy does not test the shipment-time value hypothesis.

questions.decision: The demanded outcome is shipment time. Determine whether demand, adoption and downstream capacity permit entry-time savings to affect it.

questions.title: Feedback after a simultaneous policy change
questions.stem: Proposal rework falls after an assistant launch, policy simplification and staff training happen together. Feedback mostly comes from experienced investigators. Which TWO additions best support attribution and future controlled iteration?

options.text: Train on each correction and compare rework with the month before the three changes.
options.why: Uncontrolled changes and time comparison preserve confounding.

options.text: Attribute lower rework to the assistant, treating simpler policy as support for better guidance.
options.why: Simultaneous changes cannot establish assistant attribution.

options.text: Independently score a random sample across user groups, including novices and nonresponders.
options.why: This reduces voluntary-response bias and checks actual correctness.

options.text: Track more voluntary ratings after use and narrow the satisfaction score's confidence interval.
options.why: More selected responses preserve selection bias.

options.text: Track policy version, assistant use, training and rework in matched cohorts with approved IDs.
options.why: This makes competing explanations observable.

questions.decision: The loop needs independently sampled outcome evidence and versioned exposure data; a favorable before/after change cannot identify its cause.

questions.title: Dynamic subtasks with a bounded mission
questions.stem: A fixed patent-research pipeline misses technical branches that emerge during investigation. Research is read-only, citations are required, and an analyst owns the final opinion. Which pattern best supports adaptive exploration within resource limits?

options.text: An orchestrator bounds research workers and combines citations before analyst review.
options.why: Dynamic decomposition fits unknown branches with explicit bounds.

options.text: Twelve permanent specialist stages run for every invention before analyst review.
options.why: Permanent branches add work without matching variable decomposition.

options.text: Identical agents vote on novelty; the analyst checks selected citations afterward.
options.why: Voting opinions does not ensure coverage of distinct branches.

options.text: One bounded agent follows a fixed research checklist before analyst review.
options.why: A fixed checklist preserves the demonstrated unknown-branch coverage gap.

questions.decision: The missing capability is adaptive decomposition, not simply additional model calls; keep research bounded and the legal opinion human-owned.

questions.title: Independent workers, dependent conclusions
questions.stem: Pricing, legal and safety workers review a tender in parallel. Their conclusions can conflict, but the merger keeps whichever response arrives last. Time permits parallel research, not complete sequential reviews. Which TWO changes best address this?

options.text: Require cited findings, unresolved assumptions and domain constraints in a shared output format.
options.why: Structured findings preserve constraints across independent outputs.

options.text: Let pricing merge specialist findings because it owns the proposed commercial recommendation.
options.why: Commercial ownership does not resolve legal and safety authority.

options.text: Resolve or escalate cross-domain conflicts at a synthesis gate before drafting the recommendation.
options.why: The gate handles disagreement independently of timing.

options.text: Have all workers edit a shared recommendation, with instructions to preserve existing sections.
options.why: Shared mutable prose preserves race and ownership ambiguity.

options.text: Expand context so each worker can independently draft the complete tender recommendation.
options.why: Duplicating conclusions does not define conflict resolution.

questions.decision: Parallel collection requires explicit synthesis semantics; concurrency is an execution choice, not a decision-authority rule.

questions.title: Decompose around verifiable interfaces
questions.stem: An inventory assistant mixes quantity reconciliation and narrative drafting in one prompt. Arithmetic errors are hard to trace. Reconciliation follows published rules; free-text exceptions require judgment. Which decomposition best improves auditability without autonomous investigation?

options.text: Extract cited events, apply reconciliation rules, then explain checked totals and exceptions.
options.why: Each step has an appropriate verifiable contract.

options.text: Have invoice, shipment and note agents estimate quantities, then average their discrepancies.
options.why: Averaging does not implement authoritative reconciliation rules.

options.text: Have reviewers correct complete drafts and turn edits into examples for the existing prompt.
options.why: Review can help but preserves the opaque numerical boundary.

options.text: Reason twice over each discrepancy and keep the explanation citing the most source documents.
options.why: Citation count does not validate arithmetic consistency.

questions.decision: Decompose at the numerical contract so failures become attributable and validated facts constrain the narrative.

questions.title: Capacity value without cash fiction
questions.stem: Use the exhibit. Unassisted cases are unchanged, and staffing and shipment volume stay fixed. How much monthly capacity is released, and how should finance classify it?

options.text: 450 hours; recognize equivalent payroll savings once assisted-case accuracy becomes stable.
options.why: Accuracy alone does not change staffing expenditure.

options.text: 450 hours; value redeployment separately because the pilot leaves payroll spending unchanged.
675 hours; value redeployment separately because the pilot leaves payroll spending unchanged.
options.why: This omits the additional verification minute.

options.text: 600 hours; recognize payroll savings by applying the current fully loaded hourly staff rate.
options.why: This ignores adoption and assumes nonexistent cash savings.

questions.decision: Net saving is two minutes on 13,500 adopted cases, or 450 hours; released capacity and cash savings need separate evidence.

questions.title: Requirements for a delegated search
questions.stem: Research workers may follow citations but cannot buy papers or contact authors. Citation chains exhaust budgets, and summaries lack evidence IDs. A scientist owns the final conclusion. Which THREE contract changes should precede another pilot?

options.text: Require final recommendations from every worker and choose the most detailed.
options.why: Detailed recommendations do not preserve evidence or authority.

options.text: Keep purchase and contact tools unavailable; send exceptions to the scientist.
options.why: Capability boundaries enforce the agreed delegation.

options.text: Set worker budgets and a mission deadline; report unfinished branches.
options.why: Budgets bound exploration without hiding incompleteness.

options.text: Add workers and use majority agreement to decide when coverage is sufficient.
options.why: Agreement does not enforce cost or coverage bounds.

options.text: Require stable evidence IDs and uncertainty fields in worker outputs.
options.why: Typed evidence prevents unsupported synthesis.

questions.decision: Exploration remains dynamic, but budget, evidence and authority must be deterministic parts of delegation.

questions.title: When critique is a useful loop
questions.stem: Grant summaries must meet an evidence rubric, accessibility criteria and a strict word limit. Targeted feedback improves results, but one-shot drafts omit links. Two extra calls are affordable. Which pattern best fits?

options.text: Route by grant category to a specialist writer, keeping one-shot drafting for each summary.
options.why: Routing may specialize tone but does not implement revision feedback.

options.text: Generate three independent drafts and send the median-length response to the grant officer.
options.why: Median length does not measure rubric compliance.

options.text: Revise against the rubric within a call limit; check word count and evidence links in code.
options.why: Measurable feedback supports bounded iterative revision.

options.text: Let an open-ended agent inspect previous grants until it considers the draft complete.
options.why: The task already has clear criteria and revision bounds.

questions.decision: An evaluator-optimizer fits clear, actionable quality criteria; deterministic checks cover exact constraints and iteration limits prevent uncontrolled work.

questions.title: Publish a coherent evidence generation
questions.stem: A maintenance assistant mixes new manual chapters with older appendices during a 40-minute index refresh. Answers must use one approved revision, remain reproducible, and stay available during updates. Which publication design best fits?

options.text: Apply chapter updates overnight while retaining the existing live retrieval strategy.
options.why: Time scheduling does not provide atomic coherent publication.

options.text: Keep both revisions searchable and let generation prefer newer chunks whenever their versions conflict.
options.why: Prompt preference cannot ensure complete revision coherence.

options.text: Validate a complete parallel index, atomically activate it and retain revision lineage.
options.why: Queries see a coherent validated evidence generation.

options.text: Update popular chapters first and show revision dates for technicians to check.
options.why: Dates expose but do not prevent incoherent evidence.

questions.decision: Model the index as a published evidence generation; validation and atomic activation preserve availability, coherence and reproducibility.

questions.title: A pilot that tests the business hypothesis
questions.stem: A retention assistant drafts offers; managers retain discount authority and offer rules still apply. Cancellations vary by account size and renewal quarter. Which TWO pilot commitments best test business value before adding autonomy?

options.text: Use generated-offer volume as the main outcome until cancellations become observable.
options.why: Activity is not retention or margin value.

options.text: Compare retention and margin in comparable accounts, with size slices and a fixed follow-up window.
options.why: This tests the business outcome against confounding.

options.text: Keep discount approval and policy checks; measure manager effort and offer acceptance.
options.why: This measures value within the authorized boundary.

options.text: Enable autonomous discounts when increased draft acceptance demonstrates acceptable commercial risk.
options.why: Draft acceptance does not authorize financial action.

options.text: Select accounts expected to renew and use their offer acceptance as expansion evidence.
options.why: Selection biases the evidence for retention impact.

questions.decision: Validate a measurable causal value hypothesis while preserving the pilot authority boundary; adoption is a supporting metric.

questions.title: Choose among feasible service tiers
questions.stem: Candidates share the same workload and pass security checks. Release requires correctness ≥96%, p95 ≤4 seconds and cost ≤$22/1,000 requests. Among eligible candidates, prefer correctness. Which candidate in the exhibit should be selected?

options.text: Marina: stronger correctness within latency warrants a modest per-request cost increase.
options.why: Marina exceeds the explicit budget gate.

options.text: Harbor: every gate passes, with the best correctness among feasible candidates.
options.why: Harbor passes all gates with best feasible correctness.

options.text: Jetty: lower measured cost leaves operating budget for later prompt and retrieval tuning.
options.why: Jetty fails the explicit correctness gate.

options.text: Beacon: strongest correctness improves trust despite a small completion-latency overrun.
options.why: Beacon fails the contractual latency gate.

questions.decision: Apply every release gate first, then the stated priority among feasible designs; do not silently renegotiate a gate.

questions.title: Model routing at the exception boundary
questions.stem: A cheap classifier handles routine records well but confidently mislabels ambiguous multi-entity records. A larger model improves that slice and is affordable when used selectively. Which deployment decision is best supported?

options.text: Keep the cheap classifier and escalate only when its reported confidence falls below a threshold.
options.why: Confidence is not calibrated to the failing slice.

options.text: Have the larger model rewrite explanations while keeping labels from the cheap classifier.
options.why: Explanations do not repair incorrect classification decisions.

options.text: Route multi-entity records to the larger model; check missed routes and final quality in that slice.
options.why: This targets the measured failure and validates routing.

options.text: Replace the cheap model globally because the larger model improves the difficult held-out slice.
options.why: The evidence does not justify universal extra cost.

questions.decision: Model selection applies to the complete routed system, including missed exceptions, not isolated model quality.

questions.title: A prompt contract for ambiguous evidence
questions.stem: A pension assistant sees current policy and superseded examples. It must cite evidence and distinguish missing information from ineligibility. Its template asks for confident answers. Which TWO changes best define testable behavior?

options.text: Put historical examples last so the most recent matching explanation guides policy handling.
options.why: Position cannot replace explicit evidence precedence.

options.text: Define policy precedence; require citations or an explicit insufficient-evidence response.
options.why: This establishes evidence precedence and abstention behavior.

options.text: Use high self-reported confidence as permission to resolve uncertain eligibility questions.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence cannot establish policy authority.

options.text: Separate instructions, policy metadata and source text; show conflict and missing-evidence examples.
options.why: This makes boundaries and edge behavior testable.

options.text: Request concise answers and let the model infer evidence rules from the available documents.
options.why: The required conflict behavior remains unspecified.

questions.decision: Clarify precedence, evidence and uncertainty behavior in a versioned prompt; enforce actual access and decision rights outside it.

questions.title: Select examples for a robust rule boundary
questions.stem: A triage prompt overclassifies incidents mentioning personal data when another required condition is absent. Examples cover obvious notification cases; their order changes results. Six annotated examples are available. Which revision best addresses both failures?

options.text: Select six random ordinary cases and request fuller reasoning about notification conditions.
options.why: Random ordinary examples miss the identified boundary.

options.text: State conditions, mix boundary and ordinary cases, and test held-out cases under reordered examples.
options.why: This targets the boundary and measures order robustness.

options.text: Retrieve the closest example and let semantic similarity determine the governing policy conditions.
options.why: Similarity does not establish the authoritative rule.

options.text: Use all six examples for the common personal-data subtype and retain their best-performing fixed order.
options.why: This overfits a subtype and an observed order.

questions.decision: Examples teach a contested boundary; representative coverage and held-out order variation test whether the lesson generalizes beyond a selected sequence.

questions.title: Compact history without losing the contract
questions.stem: Incident-chat summaries drop deployment IDs, rejected hypotheses and approved action scope. Investigations then repeat disproven theories or exceed authorization. Full history exceeds context limits. Which design best preserves continuity?

options.text: Keep every tool output and shorten system instructions when the conversation approaches capacity.
options.why: This trades away the behavioral contract first.

options.text: Restart after each tool call and have the operator supply the incident narrative before continuing.
options.why: This transfers state burden and invites inconsistent reconstruction.

options.text: Keep structured state for IDs, evidence, rejected theories and approved scope; retrieve details as needed.
options.why: This preserves decision-relevant state with recoverable evidence.

options.text: Keep 20 recent messages and summarize older history around the latest proposed explanation.
options.why: Recency loses binding facts and discarded hypotheses.

questions.decision: Compact around the durable incident contract rather than chat recency; source details remain retrievable.

questions.title: Reusable procedures and stable prefixes
questions.stem: Finance requests share a large policy but usually need only one specialist procedure. Changing account data precedes all procedures, increasing context and reducing cache reuse. Procedures require monthly versioned review. Which TWO changes best fit?

options.text: Use Skills with reviewed versions; find and load only the procedure needed for the task.
options.why: Progressive loading reduces unused instruction context.

options.text: Put shared policy before new account data; check actual cache writes and reads.
options.why: Stable prefixes permit measurable cache reuse.

options.text: Cache account records with shared policy and extend lifetime for cross-user reuse.
options.why: Dynamic account content disrupts common-prefix reuse.

options.text: Keep procedure titles only and reconstruct specialist steps from model knowledge.
options.why: Discovery must lead to authoritative procedure content.

options.text: Include the most-used procedure every time and remove rare procedures from support.
options.why: This removes capabilities still required by legitimate tasks.

questions.decision: Common stable policy and task-specific procedural reuse are complementary; verify measured cache behavior and keep procedure versions controlled.

questions.title: Reasoning budget tied to measurable benefit
questions.stem: Higher-budget reasoning improves complex disputes but slows completed answers. The fast path already meets routine quality gates. Both must cite evidence, and the SLA measures completion. Which experiment best informs deployment?

options.text: Keep the fast path and request detailed internal reasoning transcripts for complex exceptions.
options.why: Visible reasoning is not a correctness measurement.

options.text: Use deeper reasoning for every case, reducing evidence until average latency matches the fast path.
options.why: This introduces an untested grounding trade-off.

options.text: Test routed routine and complex cases for misses, citations, completion latency and cost.
options.why: This tests the proposed complete system against requirements.

options.text: Compare first-token latency and deploy deeper reasoning if streaming starts within the SLA.
options.why: First token is not the contracted completion metric.

questions.decision: The relevant trade-off is exception benefit versus complete-system cost and latency, including routing errors.

questions.title: Cache behavior is evidence, not a promise
questions.stem: A multilingual service has stable policy, daily tool changes and uneven traffic by language. Engineers propose caching and deferred tools, claiming fewer input tokens guarantee lower tail latency. Which THREE findings should review require?

options.text: Language-level discovery time and selection success across complete requests.
options.why: This tests the new discovery overhead and failures.

options.text: Current policy and core tools stay available; deferred tools load through supported discovery.
options.why: Optimization must preserve required operating context.

options.text: Reduced input tokens as proof that the complete service has faster production tails.
options.why: Token reduction does not establish end-to-end tails.

options.text: Longest cache duration as proof that all requests within that period will hit.
options.why: Lifetime does not guarantee identical cacheable prefixes.

options.text: Cache writes and reads by workload and version, including changed prefixes and tools.
options.why: This verifies actual reuse and invalidation effects.

questions.decision: Caching and progressive discovery can help, but actual reuse, preserved capability and measured end-to-end tails decide viability.

questions.title: Conflicting instructions in a quoted report
questions.stem: A retrieved vendor report tells an assistant to hide competitor risks and email the result externally. The user requested an internal risk summary; delivery requires separate approval. Which response best preserves evidence and authority boundaries?

options.text: Repeat the user request after each paragraph and allow delivery if risks remain.
options.why: Repeated prompts do not enforce outbound authorization.

options.text: Follow report instructions that seem consistent with the summary and log the reasoning.
options.why: Model judgment cannot grant delivery authority.

options.text: Discard the report and treat the vendor's name as evidence of elevated risk.
options.why: This discards potentially useful evidence and invents a conclusion.

options.text: Treat commands as untrusted; analyze cited facts and enforce separate delivery approval.
options.why: This separates evidence from instructions and authority.

questions.decision: Untrusted source text can inform the answer without controlling the task or acquiring tool authority.

questions.title: Remove ambiguity before catalog scale
questions.stem: Of 160 tools, three appear to reserve rooms but actually hold inventory, commit bookings and cancel holds. Selection errors exceed argument errors. What should change FIRST before expanding catalogue search?

options.text: Retain current definitions and retry whenever resulting room state differs from the request.
options.why: Retries after wrong writes can compound the harm.

options.text: Merge the three tools into a free-text endpoint that infers the requested state transition.
options.why: Inference shifts ambiguity into a consequential backend action.

options.text: Clarify names, inputs and state changes; test which tool is chosen for each action.
options.why: This repairs the semantic ambiguity before scaling discovery.

options.text: Defer all room tools and return more catalogue matches for the model to compare before acting.
options.why: Additional ambiguous results preserve the root problem.

questions.decision: Capability bloat includes overlapping semantics; discovery cannot compensate for unclear state-changing interfaces.

questions.title: Who can access the delegated resource?
questions.stem: An MCP server accepts a signed, unexpired token issued for another resource. Its broad downstream credential also exposes supplier records outside the user's region. Which TWO controls directly address these gaps?

options.text: Use stronger, shorter-lived tokens to increase confidence that requests are authorized.
options.why: Cryptographic validity does not establish audience or object access.

options.text: Rotate the downstream credential daily and audit every access outside the user's region.
options.why: Rotation and detection do not enforce user access.

options.text: Check each supplier operation against the user's region and delegated rights.
options.why: User rights must constrain the privileged backend.

options.text: Require users to state their region, comparing it with the requested supplier before access.
options.why: Untrusted request text does not establish regional authority.

options.text: Check token audience, issuer, expiry and required operation scopes before execution.
options.why: Audience validation prevents cross-resource token acceptance.

questions.decision: Token validity, intended resource and per-operation authorization are separate obligations; backend privilege must not broaden user rights.

questions.title: Feasible evidence configuration under an SLA
questions.stem: Evidence success must be ≥97% and completed-response p95 ≤3.2 seconds. Candidates share a held-out workload and access controls. The board minimizes cost after applying both gates. Which configuration in the exhibit should it select?

options.text: Delta: meets both service gates and has the lowest cost among the feasible choices.
options.why: Delta is the cheapest feasible configuration.

options.text: Alpha: best completion tail; close the quality gap after rollout.
options.why: Alpha fails the evidence-quality gate.

options.text: Beta: higher evidence success justifies its extra cost over Delta.
options.why: Beta costs more without a required quality advantage.

options.text: Gamma: strongest evidence success outweighs a small latency overrun.
options.why: Gamma fails the explicit tail gate.

questions.decision: Filter by hard gates before applying the declared cost objective; higher isolated recall is not sufficient.

questions.title: An observability contract across services
questions.stem: A regional assistant returns incomplete answers despite stable gateway p95. Gateway, retrieval and MCP logs use separate IDs and omit model versions. Unrestricted transcript collection is prohibited. Which TWO observability changes best support diagnosis?

options.text: Sample successful requests only, using customer tickets to supply evidence about failed responses.
options.why: Success-only sampling removes the relevant operational evidence.

options.text: Link approved redacted failure samples to stage outcomes; assign a regional alert owner.
options.why: Targeted evidence connects symptoms to accountable investigation.

options.text: Add gateway latency buckets and prioritize the gateway average when investigating incomplete responses.
options.why: Gateway timing misses downstream completeness and regional outcomes.

options.text: Retain complete prompts and tool payloads indefinitely to reconstruct affected customer sessions.
options.why: This conflicts with the stated privacy constraint.

options.text: Correlate stage IDs, versions, region, outcome and timing under approved access and retention.
options.why: Correlation enables localized diagnosis without blanket transcripts.

questions.decision: Correlate stages and configurations, then collect bounded failure evidence; a healthy gateway cannot establish a healthy complete service.

questions.title: A table is not a bag of paragraphs
questions.stem: Fixed-character chunks separate catalogue table values from headers, units and footnotes. Dense retrieval also finds older revisions. Product IDs and effective dates are reliable. What indexing change best addresses these failures before changing the generator?

options.text: Keep rows, units and footnotes together; index product IDs and dates for filtered retrieval.
options.why: This preserves meaning and selects the correct revision.

options.text: Summarize tables into readable prose, then discard originals after checking the summaries.
options.why: Readable summaries can lose exact row-level evidence.

options.text: Increase overlapping character windows while retaining unfiltered retrieval across all catalogue revisions.
options.why: Overlap alone does not enforce version or row semantics.

options.text: Embed values without headers so short numeric chunks rank higher for limit queries.
options.why: Values lose the context needed to interpret them.

questions.decision: Chunking must preserve the data's semantic unit, while metadata controls identifier and version precision.

questions.title: Filter structure, then retrieve the relevant account
questions.stem: Incident queries specify authoritative region, date and severity filters plus a free-text symptom. Dense retrieval crosses those boundaries; exact symptom matching misses paraphrases. Which design best satisfies both scope and semantic matching?

options.text: Retrieve globally and ask generation to discard out-of-scope incidents before answering.
options.why: Late filtering misses scope and data exposure constraints.

options.text: Predict a symptom category and use it instead of the supplied date and severity filters.
options.why: Prediction must not replace authoritative query constraints.

options.text: Match symptoms exactly inside scope; treat absent phrase matches as no relevant incident.
options.why: Exact phrases miss the demonstrated paraphrase cases.

options.text: Apply the authorized scope filters first, then match or rerank symptoms only within that set.
options.why: Hard scope precedes conceptual narrative relevance.

questions.decision: Different query components have different semantics: enforce exact scope with structured constraints and use semantic retrieval for the narrative need.

questions.title: Choose a mechanism for its actual contract
questions.stem: A nightly export has a stable authenticated REST API with status and retries. An interactive assistant needs cross-vendor discovery of approved tools with common schemas. Which TWO mechanism choices best fit?

options.text: Use a shared shell credential to give all interactive vendors a uniform command interface.
options.why: Uniform execution does not provide bounded vendor authorization.

options.text: Use MCP for approved interactive tools, with explicit schemas, server checks and operation contracts.
options.why: MCP fits shared assistant-tool capability interfaces.

options.text: Use agents for the nightly export, negotiating its format and retry behavior on each run.
options.why: Dynamic negotiation undermines the stable batch contract.

options.text: Route both paths through a large model and let prompt instructions determine protocol choice.
options.why: Prompts cannot supply absent integration contracts.

options.text: Keep the export on its authenticated API, preserving status and retry behavior.
options.why: The export is an established deterministic integration.

questions.decision: Protocol choice follows interface needs and reliability contracts; deterministic batch work does not become better through agent negotiation.

questions.title: Progressive context with an immediate core
questions.stem: Of 900 research tools, three read tools are needed almost every session. Full definitions consume context; vague rare-tool descriptions cause routing failures. Which discovery strategy best balances context, common-path latency and discoverability?

options.text: Defer every tool, including discovery, and infer needed definitions from the first user request.
options.why: Discovery must itself remain available.

options.text: Expose core tools, defer well-described rare tools and test discovery recall and session latency.
options.why: This balances common-path overhead and rare-tool discovery.

options.text: Expose core tools only and ask users to restate uncommon requests using those capabilities.
options.why: This removes legitimate rare-task coverage.

options.text: Keep every tool name in context and infer omitted argument structures and effects when needed.
options.why: Names alone make rare-tool selection and invocation unreliable.

questions.decision: Progressive discovery requires a usable immediate core and meaningful catalog descriptions; fewer context tokens alone are insufficient.

questions.title: Three distinct layers of delegated access
questions.stem: An authenticated MCP client can access other teams' onboarding cases. The server also forwards its incoming bearer token to an internal sanctions API. Which THREE integration changes support delegated access and bounded approval-sensitive actions?

options.text: Enforce team case access and approval checks against the user's permissions.
options.why: This constrains privileged backend actions to user rights.

options.text: Use separate sanctions credentials or a suitable exchange, not bearer-token forwarding.
options.why: This preserves token audience and trust boundaries.

options.text: Check that incoming MCP tokens target the compliance resource.
options.why: This establishes resource-specific token acceptance.

options.text: Require team names in prompts while retaining the existing token-forwarding path.
options.why: Prompt declarations cannot enforce identity or token boundaries.

options.text: Keep current access rules and have security audit cross-team reads weekly.
options.why: Detection leaves the demonstrated access gaps active.

questions.decision: Authentication, resource-specific token handling and object/action authorization are distinct; none can be replaced by prompt declarations or retrospective logs.

questions.title: Retrieve a change history without mixing versions
questions.stem: A safety assistant must compare warnings in two specified manual revisions. Global top-ten retrieval mixes versions and footnotes, producing a false 'no change' answer. Which design best supports the comparison?

options.text: Retrieve the two revisions separately, align sections and cite the evidence from each.
options.why: Version-scoped evidence makes the comparison reproducible.

options.text: Retrieve more global matches and infer revision order from their wording.
options.why: Similarity ranking cannot establish explicit revision scope.

options.text: Merge revisions into one summary and answer comparisons from that text.
options.why: Consolidation hides the separate evidence needed for differences.

options.text: Index only the newest manual and infer past wording from model knowledge.
options.why: Historical comparison requires historical evidence.

questions.decision: Comparison requires separately scoped evidence sets; a global semantic top-k is not a substitute for revision alignment.

questions.title: Parallelism on a real dependency graph
questions.stem: Use the fixed timings and dependencies in the exhibit. Reads cannot start before authentication; contention and retries are excluded. After parallelizing independent work, what is the shortest valid completion time?

options.text: 4.2 seconds: authenticate, parallel reads, validate, then generate.
2.4 seconds: the longest independent read determines total time.
options.why: Sequential prerequisites and dependents still contribute.

options.text: 3.8 seconds: overlap authentication with both reads, then validate and generate.
options.why: Reads cannot start before authentication.

options.text: 6.0 seconds: authenticated operations must all execute sequentially.
options.why: The two post-authentication reads are independent.

questions.decision: Parallelize sibling reads while retaining security and data dependencies; this arithmetic is a fixed-timing estimate, not a production p95 prediction.

questions.title: Discovery regression after catalog cleanup
questions.stem: After tool descriptions are shortened to internal acronyms, discovery gets faster but calibration-history tasks end in generic answers. The tool remains authorized and healthy. Which TWO checks should precede an optimization claim?

options.text: Calculate task success only among requests that found a tool, isolating catalogue-search performance.
options.why: This excludes the failing cases from evaluation.

options.text: Restore operator-facing descriptions; test discovery recall on held-out calibration requests.
options.why: This targets the observed catalog semantic regression.

options.text: Increase connection pools because faster tool search suggests failures occur after tool selection.
options.why: Evidence indicates nonselection, not backend failure.

options.text: Compare task completion and total latency, including failed searches and fallback, with the old catalogue.
options.why: This evaluates total quality and speed together.

options.text: Put calibration history in every prompt and treat successful reading as proof discovery is repaired.
options.why: This bypasses rather than tests rare-tool discovery.

questions.decision: Optimize discovery for user tasks, not only search timing; descriptions are part of the operating interface.

questions.title: Measure completion rather than convincing prose
questions.stem: A repair agent's confirmations score well, but some bookings are missing or use unauthorized locations. Release requires an authorized appointment in the requested window. Which primary evaluation best measures success?

options.text: Grade confirmation clarity and requested dates, sampling actual appointments after rollout.
options.why: This postpones verification of the release obligation.

options.text: Check the scheduling call's date and treat the resulting confirmation as booking proof.
options.why: A call does not establish successful final state.

options.text: Check final appointment state, permissions and timing, then grade confirmation accuracy.
options.why: The outcome and communicated claim must agree.

options.text: Use several judges to decide whether the transcript appears to show a successful booking.
options.why: Consensus cannot replace authoritative state verification.

questions.decision: For state-changing agents, task success is an authorized final state; transcript quality is not a proxy for execution.

questions.title: A test suite for failures that matter
questions.stem: Payroll examples mostly cover salaried staff; costly errors involve contractors, missing records and conflicting amendments. Expert annotation is limited, while total and source-ID checks are deterministic. Which TWO evaluation choices best fit?

options.text: Sample in proportion to traffic and use global accuracy to establish readiness for unusual payroll cases.
options.why: Rare critical slices can disappear in the average.

options.text: Check totals and source IDs in code; use expert disagreements to calibrate reviews and refine rubrics.
options.why: Methods match objective and subjective dimensions.

options.text: Hold out normal and risky cases, stating expected behavior for missing records and conflicting amendments.
options.why: Coverage reflects likely and consequential failure modes.

options.text: Scale annotation using identical judges and rely on majority votes instead of explicit expert criteria.
options.why: Agreement alone does not establish a calibrated rubric.

options.text: Use prompt-development examples as the release holdout because experts already approved their labels.
options.why: Reusing development cases inflates generalization evidence.

questions.decision: Combine representative coverage, deliberately difficult slices and graders matched to each requirement; preserve held-out independence.

questions.title: An experiment with a stable treatment
questions.stem: Related tickets share customers, and feedback on one affects handling of others. An earlier retrieval experiment randomized messages and changed prompts midweek. Which redesign best isolates retrieval under this interference risk?

options.text: Compare this week with last month, matching the number of messages across the two periods.
options.why: Time and case mix remain confounded.

options.text: Alternate strategies hourly and pool responses, assuming switching balances customer differences.
options.why: Related tickets can still cross contaminated treatments.

options.text: Randomize individual responses and let agents choose the prompt best suited to each customer.
options.why: Adaptive prompt choice changes the treatment.

options.text: Randomize customers, freeze other settings and prespecify outcomes, safety gates and duration.
options.why: This reduces interference and configuration confounding.

questions.decision: The experimental unit must reflect interaction dependence; a stable treatment and prespecified outcomes support interpretable evidence.

questions.title: Locate the first corrupted representation
questions.stem: Currency comparisons fail after ingestion changes. Retrieval finds the right tables and generation is unchanged, but the parser now strips currency symbols and units. What should diagnosis inspect FIRST?

options.text: Have a second model verify the narrative and accept comparisons when both cite the same document.
options.why: Shared corrupted evidence can produce agreeing errors.

options.text: Increase reasoning budget and compare existing-chunk answers before inspecting parsing or table metadata.
options.why: Reasoning cannot restore information already removed.

options.text: Compare parsed and indexed values with source tables, checking currency and unit metadata.
options.why: This tests the earliest changed representation boundary.

options.text: Use larger embeddings because expected-document retrieval may still lack financial semantic detail.
options.why: The reported lost metadata is a more direct hypothesis.

questions.decision: Diagnose upstream representation loss before tuning downstream reasoning; correct document citations can still point to corrupted values.

questions.title: Optimize the observed cost driver
questions.stem: Research costs double after stable policy moves behind a changing timestamp and full tool outputs repeat across turns. Output length is unchanged; cited evidence must remain. Which TWO experiments target the input-side changes?

options.text: Move variable content after the stable prefix; compare cache usage on matched workloads.
options.why: This tests lost reuse from prefix instability.

options.text: Halve answers and approve when output-token cost falls, without examining input usage.
options.why: Output cost is not the demonstrated changed driver.

options.text: Keep relevant passages and stable citations; retest evidence coverage and answer quality.
options.why: This targets repeated input while preserving evidence.

options.text: Use readable model summaries instead of full documents and remove original references.
options.why: Readability does not establish evidence preservation.

options.text: Add retrieval candidates to increase cache hits across related requests with different timestamps.
options.why: Candidates do not repair an unstable shared prefix.

questions.decision: Attribute the regression to measured token categories and prefix behavior before choosing optimizations.

questions.title: Monitor an outcome that arrives later
questions.stem: Immediate helpfulness stays high, but later appeals reveal wrong benefits advice for one employment category. Monitoring tracks only daily latency and ratings. Pseudonymous outcome joins are permitted for 90 days. Which change best detects this failure?

options.text: Join appeals to versioned cases; assign category alerts to policy owners within retention limits.
options.why: This captures delayed harm with reproducible configuration context.

options.text: Survey helpfulness more frequently and prioritize its daily global average for earlier detection.
options.why: Immediate global sentiment misses delayed category-specific harm.

options.text: Use response latency as an appeal warning because complex questions generally take longer.
options.why: Latency is not validated as an appeal-risk proxy.

options.text: Keep full transcripts permanently so appeals remain traceable across any later policy changes.
options.why: Permanent retention conflicts with the stated limit.

questions.decision: Operational outcomes may arrive after the interaction; monitoring needs an allowed linkage, appropriate slice and accountable response.

questions.title: Independent evidence after tuning
questions.stem: Repeated tuning raises a 300-case benchmark from 88% to 98%, yet new pilot templates fail. Engineers want to tune on pilot cases and reuse the benchmark as release evidence. Which TWO steps best separate learning from readiness measurement?

options.text: Test untouched new-template cases against fixed slice and release gates.
options.why: Independent cases estimate generalization after optimization.

options.text: Add pilot cases to the benchmark and tune until the combined score improves.
options.why: Repeated optimization contaminates the release evidence.

options.text: Use reviewed pilot failures in a development regression suite, keeping template and version labels.
options.why: Failure cases are valuable explicit regression targets.

options.text: Use judge agreement on the tuned benchmark as the final release gate.
options.why: Grader agreement does not remove case-selection leakage.

options.text: Discard the old benchmark because its high score means it has no useful cases.
options.why: Old cases still protect previously supported behavior.

questions.decision: Failures become regression assets; untouched representative cases support the release claim. Both roles matter.

questions.title: A refusal spike with an upstream cause
questions.stem: After a safety update, a prefilter blocks benign questions about account closure. Model and retrieval are unchanged, and harmful requests remain blocked. What should diagnosis do FIRST?

options.text: Test benign and harmful cases, trace false positives and validate a targeted fix.
options.why: This localizes the changed component and preserves safety.

options.text: Prompt the model to answer benign account questions despite upstream block decisions.
options.why: The prompt cannot change the upstream execution gate.

options.text: Disable the filter for all closure questions and use complaints to assess safety.
options.why: This removes protection before a targeted safety evaluation.

options.text: Replace the generator before evaluating how the changed filter handles closure cases.
options.why: The prefilter acts before generation can help.

questions.decision: Test the boundary that changed; a targeted false-positive repair is more justified than model replacement or blanket safety removal.

questions.title: Release evidence is more than a leaderboard
questions.stem: A new compliance assistant improves average correctness but introduces unauthorized retrieval and slower regional tails. Quality, access and latency have separate release gates. Which THREE findings are required before rollout?

options.text: Cross-tenant access tests pass; remaining prohibited reads block release.
options.why: Security is an independent gate.

options.text: Correctness passes on the agreed critical slices, with each tested setup fully recorded.
options.why: Quality evidence must cover slices and be reproducible.

options.text: Regional end-to-end p95 passes under load, including retrieval and retries.
options.why: The regional tail gate needs relevant measurements.

options.text: An engineering-approved weighted score offsets access failures with correctness gains.
options.why: The policy does not permit gate compensation.

options.text: Global average latency improves, with regional limits renegotiated after launch.
options.why: Average performance does not satisfy existing regional gates.

questions.decision: Independent safety and SLA obligations cannot be traded away inside a composite quality metric without an authorized policy change.

questions.title: Cache break-even under stated traffic
questions.stem: Use the fictional rates in the exhibit. One request writes a 20,000-token prefix; nine reuse it before expiry. Variable input costs are identical. What is the correct ten-request prefix-cost comparison?

options.text: $0.050 cached versus $0.400 uncached; saving $0.350.
options.why: The supplied cache-read rate is nonzero.

options.text: $0.086 cached versus $0.040 uncached; adding $0.046.
options.why: Uncached pricing applies to all ten requests.

options.text: $0.086 cached versus $0.400 uncached; saving $0.314.
$0.040 cached versus $0.400 uncached; saving $0.360.
options.why: The first request uses the stated cache-write rate.

questions.decision: The fictional prices isolate prefix economics: one write plus nine reads. Real benefit also depends on reuse and cache validity.

questions.title: A security boundary around external evidence
questions.stem: A supplier document tells a pricing assistant to retrieve internal margins and include them in a supplier-facing draft. Buyers may access margins separately, but this task is an internal procurement comparison. Which design best contains the attack?

options.text: Permit existing tools when an injection detector reports low attack probability.
options.why: Detection alone leaves broad consequential capabilities available.

options.text: Restrict data/tool flows to the authorized task; treat supplier commands as content.
options.why: Task-scoped capabilities bound the attack's effect.

options.text: Have another model approve the draft if margin values have citations.
options.why: Cited disclosure can still be unauthorized disclosure.

options.text: Let supplier text drive retrieval but require buyer approval for drafts mentioning margins.
options.why: Draft review does not constrain unauthorized retrieval.

questions.decision: Content screening supports defense, but the trusted task and enforced data-flow permissions determine what the assistant can do.

questions.title: Two failures hidden by one success rate
questions.stem: A scholarship assistant has stable overall accuracy but more unsupported rejections and appeals for translated records. Reviewers sometimes accept fluent explanations without checking evidence. Which TWO evaluations best distinguish coverage gaps from reviewer overreliance?

options.text: Add translated examples to the live prompt and assess them through overall reviewer acceptance.
options.why: Acceptance can reflect the stated overreliance.

options.text: Match positive-recommendation counts by language and use the existing overall accuracy metric.
options.why: Equal quotas do not diagnose either failure mode.

options.text: Audit accepted and corrected unsupported advice using cited evidence and a calibrated rubric.
options.why: This tests human oversight effectiveness.

options.text: Compare explanation length by language, using longer answers to indicate adequate consideration.
options.why: Length does not measure evidence or decision quality.

options.text: Score language and translation slices against independent labels, including missing-evidence behavior.
options.why: This tests coverage and grounding disparities.

questions.decision: Separate model/data failures from oversight failures; an overall success rate can conceal both and is insufficient for expansion.

questions.title: Approval when evidence has changed
questions.stem: An analyst approves a loan adjustment using income evidence. A refresh changes income and the proposed adjustment, but approval is attached only to the case ID. Which design preserves approval authority without restarting unrelated work?

options.text: Notify the analyst of the revised adjustment and execute after a short opportunity to object.
options.why: Silence does not establish approval of changed terms.

options.text: Reuse approval when a second model finds the recommendation label unchanged despite new evidence.
options.why: Matching labels can hide material changed amounts.

options.text: Bind approval to the exact adjustment and evidence version; obtain new review after relevant changes.
options.why: Approval must cover the operation that executes.

options.text: Reuse case approval within the same product category, logging the changed income for later review.
options.why: Product category is too coarse for consequential approval.

questions.decision: Human approval needs a concrete subject and invalidation rule; bind it to the material decision state.

questions.title: Regulated processing is a full data flow
questions.stem: A clinical assistant's inference provider offers an appropriate BAA, but full documents also reach a separate tracing vendor and unrestricted engineer exports. Which TWO prerequisites address these gaps before a PHI pilot?

options.text: Map where PHI flows across services and exports; check each required agreement and safeguard.
options.why: The entire PHI flow needs review.

options.text: Test approved access and retention for analytics and workspaces before any PHI pilot starts.
options.why: This closes the concrete uncontrolled copies.

options.text: Apply the inference BAA to analytics and engineer exports serving the same clinical purpose.
options.why: One provider agreement does not cover other processors.

options.text: Use draft-only model operation as sufficient protection for copies in analytics and exports.
options.why: Read-only inference still processes and discloses PHI.

options.text: Pilot with full documents and de-identify archived traces after debugging needs are known.
options.why: This exposes information before controls are validated.

questions.decision: Provider eligibility is one input; agreements, minimum necessary access and safeguards must cover the actual complete processing flow.

questions.title: Fairness evidence before a policy intervention
questions.stem: A hiring assistant matches recruiters 94% of the time, but one protected group gets fewer interviews. Historical labels may be biased, and job requirements vary by role. What should governance do before changing recommendation policy?

options.text: Maximize historical agreement separately for each group as the fairness target.
options.why: Historical bias would become the target.

options.text: Equalize every role's interview rates before inspecting requirements or labels.
options.why: Blind parity ignores relevant role and policy context.

options.text: Exclude protected attributes and declare fairness once prompts no longer include them explicitly.
options.why: Proxies and historical bias can remain.

options.text: Agree role-specific fairness goals with legal and hiring; audit labels and alternatives.
options.why: This examines biased labels and relevant policy criteria.

questions.decision: Fairness needs an agreed context-specific assessment and trustworthy labels; neither historical agreement nor attribute removal proves it.

questions.title: Safer failure under ambiguous tool state
questions.stem: A benefits service sometimes accepts applications before its response times out. Fresh retries create duplicates and may jeopardize the original filing date. Staff can inspect durable records. Which recovery design best fits?

options.text: Retry with new IDs and let staff later choose the earliest accepted application.
options.why: Duplicates still create consequential processing conflicts.

options.text: Ask applicants to restart and rely on name-based duplicate detection.
options.why: This shifts uncertainty and can lose application continuity.

options.text: Infer acceptance from elapsed time and send a provisional success message.
options.why: Timing cannot establish authoritative submission state.

options.text: Keep one submission ID; reconcile status, show pending and escalate if unresolved.
options.why: This prevents blind duplicate submission and preserves continuity.

questions.decision: Unknown execution outcome is a distinct state; durable reconciliation and idempotency are safer than guessing success or repeating writes.

questions.title: Human review that can withstand demand
questions.stem: A fraud threshold improves recall but doubles review volume. Staffing is fixed and urgent cases already approach deadlines. Reviewers need evidence and time to override. Which TWO requirements should govern rollout?

options.text: Hide uncertainty to speed reviewers while retaining the model's proposed fraud classification.
options.why: This weakens informed review and challenge.

options.text: Test evidence presentation, override powers and overload escalation under realistic time limits.
options.why: This tests meaningful review rather than nominal approval.

options.text: Approve the better-recall threshold and request staff after the larger queue becomes measurable.
options.why: Current capacity is already binding.

options.text: Adopt overdue model recommendations automatically to prevent delays in fraud-case disposition.
options.why: Queue delay cannot grant consequential authority.

options.text: Test fraud capture and false positives against review capacity, queue age and urgent deadlines.
options.why: Oversight must remain operationally feasible.

questions.decision: Human oversight is a capacity-constrained control whose effectiveness requires evidence, authority and realistic response time.

questions.title: A valid erasure request across derived artifacts
questions.stem: Legal confirms a scoped erasure request. Personal data exists in records, search chunks, vector metadata, traces and backups with approved restore procedures. Only the application record was deleted. What guidance best completes the request?

options.text: Delete plaintext only, retaining embeddings because mathematical transformation removes their personal-data character.
options.why: Embeddings and metadata are not categorically exempt.

options.text: Retain production search entries until backup expiry, then delete all stores together.
options.why: This leaves in-scope active processing untreated.

options.text: Delete every historical artifact immediately, including records covered by approved retention exceptions.
options.why: The confirmed scope includes legally determined exceptions.

options.text: Erase in-scope derived copies and prevent their return during approved backup restoration.
options.why: Derived artifacts and restore paths remain within scope.

questions.decision: Apply the legally confirmed scope to actual derived copies and restoration behavior; storage format alone does not settle identifiability.

questions.title: Transparent assistance without irrelevant exposure
questions.stem: Residents mistake a benefits assistant's explanations for official determinations. Case details and security prompts are protected. Which TWO changes best improve understanding without relying solely on a disclaimer?

options.text: Treat acceptance of a registration notice as sufficient evidence that residents understand the service.
options.why: Registration acknowledgement does not establish ongoing understanding.

options.text: Present high confidence scores as evidence that explanations are provisional official determinations.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence does not establish authority.

options.text: Publish internal prompts and access rules so residents can inspect each decision.
options.why: This exposes unnecessary internal security material.

options.text: Test what users understand in real journeys; change the interface and escalation route if needed.
options.why: This tests effectiveness rather than disclaimer presence.

options.text: Label advice, cite policy and show official decision and appeal routes.
options.why: This clarifies the service's authority and recourse.

questions.decision: Transparency should explain evidence, authority and recourse, then be tested with users; it need not expose security or private case details.

questions.title: Discovery before accepting an automation promise
questions.stem: An executive wants half the order cycle time. The assistant speeds entry, but warehouses have picking queues. Substitution authority is disputed, and stage timings and exception demand are unknown. What should discovery do FIRST?

options.text: Accept the target and select a framework extensible to entry and warehouse agents.
options.why: Framework choice precedes essential requirements.

options.text: Map bottlenecks, baselines and substitution authority with affected teams before scoping.
options.why: The value bottleneck and authority remain unestablished.

options.text: Confirm the executive's target and align operational teams after architecture approval.
options.why: The conflicting operational constraints remain unresolved.

options.text: Estimate from an entry prototype, treating warehouse capacity as outside scope.
options.why: This could optimize a nonbinding stage.

questions.decision: Structured discovery establishes the real bottleneck and decision authority before a credible scope or outcome commitment.

questions.title: Explain a trade-off with a decision trigger
questions.stem: A workflow meets current retail needs and an eight-week deadline. An agent handles exploratory exceptions better but needs operational testing. Which TWO ADR elements best justify the choice and define when to revisit it?

options.text: Compare every framework feature and leave the recommendation open until implementers agree.
options.why: This avoids the required architectural decision.

options.text: Set measurable revisit triggers for exception volume and quality, with an evidence owner.
options.why: This makes reconsideration accountable and evidence-driven.

options.text: Explain the choice through current coverage, deadline, risk and the agent alternative's limits.
options.why: This explains why the decision fits current constraints.

options.text: Promise eventual agent adoption when a newer model becomes available to the business.
options.why: Model availability does not establish business need.

options.text: Declare the workflow permanent so teams can stop tracking future exception demand.
options.why: This blocks justified lifecycle reconsideration.

questions.decision: A useful decision record connects evidence and constraints to a choice, then names the conditions and owner for reconsideration.

questions.title: An SLA dispute about the clock
questions.stem: The SLA requires a useful answer within five seconds. The dashboard measures only generation, excluding authentication, retrieval and retries. Partners report breaches; product and operations dispute ownership. What should happen FIRST?

options.text: Agree what completion and failure mean, time the full path and name the SLA owner.
options.why: This aligns measurement with the agreed service outcome.

options.text: Relabel model time and leave contract assessment to integration vendors.
options.why: This leaves the end-to-end obligation unowned.

options.text: Shorten model output to offset an estimated average allowance for authentication and tools.
options.why: Estimated averages do not define the contractual tail.

options.text: Sum independent component p95s and judge teams compliant when their own targets pass.
options.why: Summed marginal p95s are not an end-to-end distribution.

questions.decision: Define and own the user-visible SLI first; isolated generation speed cannot resolve a measurement and accountability mismatch.

questions.title: The receiving team needs an operating contract
questions.stem: A prototype's author manually refreshes sources, interprets tool failures and remembers tested versions. A platform team takes production ownership next month. Which TWO handoff artifacts are most essential?

options.text: An archive of exploratory prompts from which receiving operators choose a reliable configuration.
options.why: This leaves evaluated configuration ambiguous.

options.text: An immediate feature-expansion plan so the receiving team learns operation through development.
options.why: Expansion is not a substitute for operating readiness.

options.text: Demo recordings and slides from which receiving operators infer configuration and recovery steps.
options.why: A demo omits the described manual operations.

options.text: Give tested incident and rollback steps, clear owners and alert paths; rehearse with the receiving team.
options.why: This establishes executable operating ownership.

options.text: Document supported versions, deployment and refresh gates, and behavior when each process fails.
options.why: This transfers reproducible implementation knowledge.

questions.decision: Handoff requires reproducible configuration and rehearsed operating procedures, not only knowledge that a prototype can succeed.

questions.title: Iteration after a policy revision
questions.stem: Finance urgently changes one region's expense policy. Engineers want a quick live prompt edit, but releases require finance behavior validation and operations acceptance. Which lifecycle action best fits?

options.text: Edit the prompt live and have finance review later, classifying the short change as documentation.
options.why: Behavior changes still require validation.

options.text: Freeze policy changes until the next model upgrade because current regressions establish reliability.
options.why: This preserves outdated policy behavior unnecessarily.

options.text: Retrieve the policy dynamically and remove finance approval because the prompt remains unchanged.
options.why: A new evidence policy still changes behavior and authority.

options.text: Version the change, add regional cases, obtain required validation and release with rollback.
options.why: Urgency can use a controlled targeted change path.

questions.decision: Iteration is governed by behavioral impact and ownership, not the number of edited words or whether the prompt file changes.

questions.title: Resolve the meaning of a requirement
questions.stem: 'Real-time' means two-second first token to operations and ten-second evidence-backed completion to analysts. Safety requires escalation of uncertain equipment instructions. No service definition is approved. What discovery activity should precede design estimates?

options.text: Use stakeholder journeys to agree completion, uncertainty handling and timing acceptance criteria.
options.why: This resolves the contradictory meaning of success.

options.text: Provide separate dashboards so each group can monitor its preferred interpretation while design proceeds.
options.why: Separate dashboards preserve conflicting obligations.

options.text: Choose the two-second target for all interactions and estimate the largest fast-streaming model.
options.why: First token and useful completion remain confused.

options.text: Demonstrate a ten-second completed answer and seek agreement on timing after the quality is visible.
options.why: A demonstration does not resolve escalation or contractual acceptance.

questions.decision: Translate vague labels into shared observable behavior before architecture commitments; uncertainty behavior is part of the service contract.

questions.title: Expansion after a narrowly successful pilot
questions.stem: A claims pilot passes for one product and language. A new unit has different rules, data rights and higher peak load but the same interface. Which TWO commitments best support expansion?

options.text: Copy the existing prompt and use first-month satisfaction to validate the new unit's rules.
options.why: Unvalidated rules expose users before readiness evidence.

options.text: Compare rules, rights, workload and risk to identify which prior evidence transfers.
options.why: This distinguishes reusable evidence from new assumptions.

options.text: Discard initial pilot metrics because different rules invalidate all prior evidence.
options.why: Reusable components can retain relevant evidence.

options.text: Agree new slice and load gates; expand with rollback preserving the validated service.
options.why: This validates changed scope without destroying the baseline.

options.text: Roll out globally after interface approval and add governance when incidents warrant it.
options.why: Interface similarity does not establish readiness.

questions.decision: Expansion is a scope change; preserve valid evidence and explicitly validate what the new context changes.

questions.title: Communicating uncertainty in the executive case
questions.stem: A volunteer pilot cuts sales drafting time 40%. Users are experienced, complex deals are excluded and revenue effects are unknown. Leadership wants to announce 40% higher sales productivity. What should the architect communicate?

options.text: Withhold the drafting benefit until a full revenue cycle finishes.
options.why: This discards a valid measured intermediate gain.

options.text: Combine word-count gains with drafting savings to estimate total productivity.
options.why: Word count is not overall business productivity.

options.text: Forecast 40% for all staff with a disclaimer about experienced volunteers.
options.why: A disclaimer does not justify extrapolation.

options.text: Report drafting gains and pilot limits; test wider claims against representative outcomes.
options.why: This states supported results and the missing evidence.

questions.decision: Communicate measured benefits at their actual scope and maturity, then identify the evidence needed for broader claims.

questions.title: A lifecycle contract for retrieval updates
questions.stem: Policy owners update sources independently. The platform owns uptime and policy teams own correctness, but nobody owns index freshness or refresh recovery. Current-index tests pass. Which TWO handoff additions address ongoing responsibility?

options.text: Treat manual policy-update notices to users as sufficient protection against indexing delays.
options.why: Users still receive stale assistant evidence.

options.text: Record lineage and rollback so invalid updates cannot displace the last validated evidence.
options.why: This makes updates reproducible and recoverable.

options.text: Assign freshness, validation and failed-refresh owners, with alert and escalation routes.
options.why: Freshness becomes an owned operating obligation.

options.text: Transfer model tuning to operations because a correct current index rules out future data faults.
options.why: Future source and indexing failures remain possible.

options.text: Survey accuracy quarterly without source versions to focus on user outcomes over implementation.
options.why: The survey cannot diagnose or recover specific invalid updates.

questions.decision: Correctness depends on an ongoing data lifecycle; handoff must assign freshness, validation, version lineage and recovery responsibilities.

questions.title: Team policy versus local preference
questions.stem: Teams need shared Claude Code conventions, while production deployments require central permission controls. A proposal puts prohibitions in project instructions and allows broad shell execution. Which setup best fits?

options.text: Version shared coding guidance and use managed rules plus scoped credentials for production limits.
options.why: Instructions guide work; permissions enforce capability boundaries.

options.text: Acknowledge policy at session start while retaining unrestricted credentials for approved production work.
options.why: Acknowledgement does not constrain the available authority.

options.text: Put restrictions in repository instructions and allow developers to grant broad shell access locally.
options.why: Local permission can bypass the instructed prohibition.

options.text: Replace project guidance with shell deny rules so style and safety requirements use one mechanism.
options.why: Permission rules do not express coding conventions well.

questions.decision: Use project instructions for conventions and managed permission/credential boundaries for prohibited operations; each serves a different function.

questions.title: Improve the complete engineering workflow
questions.stem: AI-generated PRs arrive faster, but broad changes, unrelated tests and unclear intent increase review time. Release lead time is unchanged. Which workflow change best improves overall productivity?

options.text: Run more parallel sessions and measure PRs produced per engineer.
options.why: More output can worsen the review queue.

options.text: Scope reviewable, acceptance-tested changes; measure review effort and merge lead time.
options.why: This targets the downstream review bottleneck.

options.text: Generate longer explanations and complete file snapshots for reviewers.
options.why: More material does not ensure focused reviewability.

options.text: Allow assistant self-approval after tests, limiting human review to incident-prone files.
options.why: Test success does not transfer maintainer authority.

questions.decision: Optimize the end-to-end delivery process and reviewability, not a local drafting-time metric.

questions.title: A debugging incident with a permission boundary
questions.stem: A staging diagnostic reads synthetic fixtures, but its wrapper also accesses protected credentials. Managed policy blocks execution. Which TWO actions best restore useful diagnostics under the existing policy?

options.text: Disable managed restrictions until the diagnostic finishes and inspect logs for unwanted access.
options.why: Retrospective logs do not preserve the execution boundary.

options.text: Copy protected credentials to a staging path the diagnostic can already read.
options.why: This defeats the protected data boundary.

options.text: Run the smallest permitted diagnostic and tell its owner which wrapper path caused the block.
options.why: This restores useful debugging with accountable repair.

options.text: Use an allow hook to override the managed deny for this staging investigation.
options.why: Managed deny controls are not overridden by an allow hook.

options.text: Separate fixture diagnosis from secret access and retain only the rights needed for the investigation.
options.why: This removes unnecessary protected access.

questions.decision: Diagnose the operation that triggers enforcement and remove unnecessary capability; do not use hooks or copied secrets to bypass policy.

questions.title: A quality gate that is executable
questions.stem: A coding assistant sometimes skips the required formatter or targeted tests. Both checks already exist in CI. What adjustment best makes completion dependable?

options.text: Have another assistant approve when the conversation claims checks ran.
options.why: Conversation review still relies on unverified claims.

options.text: Retain guidance, enforce CI checks and use hooks for earlier feedback.
options.why: Deterministic gates enforce the requirement independently of prose.

options.text: Add repeated reminders and require an explicit completion statement.
options.why: Repeated claims do not establish actual check outcomes.

options.text: Bypass CI for small assistant patches because instructions cover them.
options.why: Patch size does not prove required checks passed.

questions.decision: Guidance explains the workflow; existing executable gates establish completion. Hooks can shorten feedback without replacing CI authority.

drills.title: Index release review
drills.stem: Judge each proposal independently: does it meet the stated evidence-publication requirement? No fixed number of Yes answers is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: one approved revision per answer. Proposal: validate a complete new index and atomically activate its revision pointer.
rows.why: A coherent evidence generation prevents mixed revision answers.

rows.text: Requirement: reproduce old answers. Proposal: store only the latest source text, retaining document names for historical citations.
rows.why: Names do not recover the historical evidence version.

rows.text: Requirement: authorized retrieval. Proposal: select documents first and hide forbidden citations only when formatting the response.
rows.why: Unauthorized content must not enter the assistant context.

rows.text: Requirement: detect failed refreshes. Proposal: alert on incomplete indexing with a named owner and continue serving the validated generation.
rows.why: The proposal contains failure and assigns a response.

rows.text: Requirement: measure full completion tails. Proposal: use the model first-token histogram as the sole acceptance gate.
rows.why: First token is different from complete response latency.

drills.title: Value and oversight judgments
drills.stem: Judge whether each inference follows from the stated evidence, independently of the other rows.

rows.text: A pilot releases staff capacity while staffing is unchanged; the released hours alone establish equivalent immediate payroll savings.
rows.why: Capacity and cash expenditure are different outcomes.

rows.text: A larger model improves a difficult slice; evaluating routing errors is necessary before claiming a routed system preserves that benefit.
rows.why: Missed exceptions can prevent the larger model from helping.

rows.text: A human review queue exceeds its deadline; the existence of reviewers alone establishes that oversight remains effective.
rows.why: Review capacity and timeliness constrain effective oversight.

rows.text: A policy and assistant change together; versioned comparable cohorts and independent outcome adjudication strengthen causal interpretation.
rows.why: They make competing explanations and actual outcomes observable.

rows.text: A cache test counts prefix writes and reads; fictional prices can support arithmetic without claiming those are current platform prices.
rows.why: Supplied assumptions define the exercise, not current billing.

drills.title: Choose the missing contract
drills.stem: Select the primary missing contract for each situation. Choices may repeat.

rows.text: A generated answer cites a manual name, but the team cannot identify the manual revision used.
A model sees a procurement record because the service credential is broader than the requesting user.
rows.why: The user access boundary is missing.

rows.text: A correct benchmark is repeatedly tuned until it passes, then presented as untouched release evidence.
rows.why: Optimization has contaminated the claimed holdout.

rows.text: A document refresh fails and neither the source owner nor platform team accepts the alert.
rows.why: An accountable failure responder is missing.

rows.text: An analyst approves one adjustment amount, but a different amount executes under the case-level approval.
rows.why: Approval does not cover the executed operation.
